O substantivo: sem artigos e o gênero pe: The noun: no articles, and gender from the last letter
PASSO 1: Antes de mais nada: o que é um: STEP 1: First of all: what is a noun? You have heard the word «noun» a thousand times at school. But let me refresh your memory, because it matters for what comes next. A noun is a word that names. It names things, people, places, ideas, feelings. House. Map. Dog. Friendship. Coffee. Brazil. It is the «who» or the «what» of any sentence. If you can point at something and give it a name, that name is a noun. In English you hardly think about it. You learned the language so naturally that a noun is just one word among others. But when you learn a new language, you need to understand what a noun is, because it is the basis of everything. And in Russian the noun has one property that will determine everything that comes after: gender. STEP 2: The first piece of good news: Russian has no articles. Here you can breathe a sigh of relief. Russian has no articles. Neither definite («the») nor indefinite («a», «an»). Nothing. In English we say «the map» or «a house». The article is a separate little word. In Russian there is none. Дом can mean «house», «the house» or «a house». Context decides. You do not have to worry about any article. Zero. But this raises a question. In English, nouns have no grammatical gender, so you never had to ask who decides it. In Russian every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the adjectives and verbs agree with it. So the inevitable question: who decides the gender? STEP 3: Who decides the Russian gender: the last letter. The direct answer: the last letter of the word. It determines the gender. No article, no exception, no discussion. And here is the second novelty: Russian has three genders, not two. • 1. Masculine — he (он) • 2. Feminine — she (она) • 3. Neuter — it (оно) — the English «it», where things, objects and concepts live. You may have heard that Russian has a «neuter gender». This is it: a third box for the words that are neither masculine nor feminine. Notice that in Russian a table can be «he» and a book can be «she»: gender is a property of the word, not of the thing.
Gênero pela terminação: tabela e regra d: Gender from the ending: the table and the three-second rule
A tabela mestra: o gênero pela terminaçã: The master table: gender from the ending. Here is the rule that solves 95% of cases. Look at the last letter. Apply the table. Done. That is all. Ends in a consonant? Masculine. Ends in -а or -я? Feminine. Ends in -о, -е or -мя? Neuter. Ends in -ь? You need to check the dictionary, and I will explain why in a moment. The three-second protocol. For any new word you meet, do this: • 1. Look at the last letter. • 2. Apply the rule: consonant or -й → masculine -а or -я → feminine -о, -е or -мя → neuter -ь → dictionary • 3. Write the word down together with its gender. Always. Never memorise a Russian word without the gender. The right flashcard is not «дом = house». It is «дом = house (masculine)». The gender always comes with the word, because, as you will see in the next lesson, the adjective depends on it. Does it look simple? It is simple. But there are some traps. And that is what we will talk about now.

PASSO 1: ARMADILHA Nº 1 — O sinal brando: STEP 1: TRAP No. 1 — The soft sign (-ь). The -ь (called the «soft sign» or «мягкий знак») is the stone in the Russian learner's shoe. It has no sound of its own. It is not a vowel and not a consonant. It is a sign that softens the consonant before it. Think of it as a «seasoning» that changes the texture of the sound but adds nothing. The problem is that, for gender, it is ambiguous. Some nouns ending in -ь are masculine. Others are feminine. There is no rule and no logic. You have to check the dictionary. See: How do you know? Only by looking in the dictionary. But do not despair. With time you will hear the gender, because the adjectives that go with the word give the game away. A Russian says большо́й день («a big day») and больша́я ночь («a big night»). The ending of the adjective tells you whether it is masculine or feminine. But that is a topic for the next lesson. For now, remember this: -ь means dictionary. Do not try to guess. Check. And write the gender down with the word. STEP 2: TRAP No. 2 — The -мя. Words ending in -мя are neuter. Always. And there are few of them: about ten in the whole Russian language. You do not need to memorise them all at once. The two most used are: имя (EE-mya) — name время (VRYEH-mya) — time, hour The others (знамя, семя, пламя, стремя, племя, темя, бремя, вымя, полымя) are less frequent. But the rule is the same: -мя = neuter. You have just learned the rule for all of them at once. That is what a rule is for: it works even with words you have never seen. STEP 3: TRAP No. 3 — The celebrity кофе. Here is the most famous exception in the Russian language. Ко́фе (KOH-fyeh) — coffee. It ends in -е. By the rule it should be neuter. But it is masculine. Why? History. The word entered Russian as кофий (KOH-fee), which was masculine. Over time the word shrank to кофе, but the gender stayed. It is a linguistic fossil. Remember: вку́сный ко́фе (tasty coffee). Not «вкусное кофе». It is masculine. (Modern grammars tolerate the neuter in informal contexts, but the masculine is the classic, recommended form. Use the masculine.)
Em português dizemos «o livro» e «um liv: In English we say «the book» and «a book». In Russian there is no «the», «a» or «an»: the word «книга» can mean «the book» or «a book», and the context decides. That is why, for every noun, you need to remember the gender (masculine, feminine or neuter). It is the gender that controls the adjective, the possessive and the verb in the past.

There are exceptions, and they matter because they name males. па́па (PAH-pah) — dad де́душка (DYEH-doosh-kah) — grandpa дя́дя (DYAH-dya) — uncle мужчи́на (moozh-CHEE-nah) — man ю́ноша (YOO-noh-shah) — young man судья́ (soo-DYAH) — judge ста́роста (STAH-rah-stah) — group leader, class monitor во́евода (VOH-ee-vah-dah) — military commander (historical) влади́ка (vlah-DEE-kah) — lord, sovereign Ники́та (nee-KEE-tah) — Nikita (male name) Илья́ (ee-LYAH) — Ilya (male name) Лёва (LYOH-vah) — Liova (short for Lev) Са́ша (SAH-shah) — Sasha (short for Aleksandr or Aleksandra) Же́ня (ZHEH-nyah) — Zhenia (short for Evgenii or Evgeniia) All of them end in -а or -я, but they are masculine, because they name men. The ending rule holds for most words, but meaning wins for living beings. It is an exception you use every day, so remember it. STEP 2: TRAP No. 5 — дитя, the child. Дитя́ (dee-TYAH) — child. It is the only neuter word that names a person. All the other words that name people are masculine or feminine. Дитя is the single exception. It is worth knowing because it is a common word. STEP 3: TRAP No. 6 — Nouns of two genders. Some words can be masculine or feminine, depending on the sex of the person they name: сирота́ (see-rah-TAH) — orphan (boy or girl) у́мница (OOM-nee-tsah) — clever boy or girl пья́ница (PYAH-nee-tsah) — drunkard (man or woman) о́бжора (OHB-zhah-rah) — glutton (man or woman) бродя́га (brah-DYAH-gah) — vagabond (man or woman) самоуби́йца (sah-mah-oo-BEE-tsah) — a person who takes their own life (man or woman) The word does not change; the adjective that goes with it reveals the gender. But that is a topic for the next lesson. STEP 4: TRAP No. 7 — Loanwords. Foreign words that enter Russian sometimes do not follow the rules. The main ones: Ending in -и, -у, -ю → usually neuter: такси́ (tahk-SEE; taxi), меню́ (myeh-NYOO; menu), киви́ (KEE-vee; kiwi), желе́ (zheh-LEH; jelly), кафе́ (kah-FEH; café, but careful: кофе is masculine and кафе is neuter!), метро́ (meh-TROH; metro), кино́ (kee-NOH; cinema), пальто́ (pahl-TOH; coat), бюро́ (byoo-ROH; office) Naming women → feminine, whatever the ending: ле́ди (lady), Мэ́ри (Mary), Ма́ргарет (Margaret), Э́лен (Ellen). Animals are masculine: кенгуру́ (kyen-goo-ROO; kangaroo), по́ни (pony) Ending in -о and naming males → masculine: маэ́стро (maestro), импреса́рио (impresario). Place names in -о, such as Токи́о (Tokyo), are neuter. Each case is its own case. But the most common is: a loanword ending in a vowel other than -а/-я → neuter.
A GRANDE DIVERGÊNCIA: português vs. russ: THE BIG DIVERGENCE: English vs. Russian

THE BIG DIVERGENCE: English vs. Russian. Here lives the number one confusion for English speakers. It is rarely explained clearly, so let us go straight to the point: in English, things have no gender. A table, a house, a book are all «it». In Russian every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and it does not matter what the thing is. See the table. On the left, the English word and what English calls it. On the right, the Russian word and its gender. Notice that there is nothing to «match», because English has no grammatical gender to match. The doctrine of this lesson in one sentence: in Russian, gender belongs to the word, not to the thing. Дом is masculine because in Russian it is masculine. Full stop. This is not a detail. It is the difference between speaking Russian and speaking English with Russian words. You are studying another language. Its rules are its own, not yours.
Olhe a última letra do substantivo no si: Look at the last letter of the noun in the singular. Masculine: ends in a consonant (стол, дом), in -й (музей) or in -ь (день, словарь). Feminine: ends in -а or -я (книга, неделя), or in -ь (ночь, тетрадь). Neuter: ends in -о, -е or -мя (окно, море, имя, время). Step by step: (1) look at the last letter; (2) if it is -ь, check the list or the dictionary; (3) check whether there is a suffix that gives the gender away (-тель, -ость, -ие...). Two cautions: (1) words in -ь can be masculine or feminine and there is no rule, so memorise the gender with the word; (2) men whose word ends in -а or -я are masculine: папа, дедушка, дядя, мужчина.

THE BIG SURPRISE: the words where «it» in English hides a gender. This section is usually missing from grammars, but it is the one you will use most. English has «he», «she» and «it», and for things you always say «it». Your brain has an autopilot: a book, a car, a table are all «it». In Russian, that autopilot lets you down, because every one of those things is secretly masculine, feminine or neuter, and nothing in English tells you which. Do not assume that «it» means neuter. Neuter is just one of three boxes: a car is feminine, a table is masculine, a window is neuter. The only reliable guide is the ending. English gives no clue about gender: a thing is just «it». In Russian the gender belongs to the word, so read the ending. STEP 16: • 6. The English «it» hides a gender.
